title: Ceramic vs. Porcelain Tile Flooring: Key Differences Explained
meta: Porcelain absorbs under 0.5% water and wears harder; ceramic costs less and cuts easier. Wills Flooring on PEI ratings, rectified edges, wet rooms and cost.
keywords: ceramic vs porcelain tile, porcelain vs ceramic tile flooring, PEI rating tile, rectified tile, large format tile installation, tile flooring Lynnwood

blocks.lead: Porcelain is the better floor tile for almost every room because it absorbs under 0.5 percent water and wears harder; ceramic wins on price, easier cutting and walls.
blocks.detail: Both are fired clay and both are installed the same way, so the choice is about where the tile lives. Wills Flooring prices tile from a measured layout, so this post explains what drives cost rather than quoting a rate.

blocks.html: "Is porcelain really worth the extra money over ceramic?" is one of the most common tile questions we hear in Lynnwood and Mill Creek kitchens, and the honest answer is that it depends on the room and the tile size. The two materials are cousins, not twins. Here is what actually separates them, what the ratings on the box mean, and where each one belongs.

blocks.note: Look for a certified porcelain mark on the box. Some imported tile uses the word loosely, and the absorption number is what counts.

blocks.text: PEI ratings: read the number, not the marketing

blocks.html: PEI is an abrasion test of the glaze, not the body. It tells you how much foot traffic the surface takes before it dulls. Both ceramic and porcelain carry PEI ratings, and a PEI 4 ceramic will outwear a PEI 2 porcelain on a floor.

head: PEI
Rated for
Where we use it
rows: Bathroom floors used in bare feet or slippers
Entries, mudrooms, family kitchens with dogs
Garages and shops; overkill for most homes but fine

items.title: Bathrooms and showers
items.text: Porcelain's low absorption means the tile itself will not hold moisture, but it does not make a shower waterproof. Waterproofing is the membrane behind and under the tile. We use porcelain on floors, either tile on walls, and always a proper membrane.

items.title: Mudrooms and entries
items.text: Wet boots, road grit and dog paws in an Everett or Bothell entry are the hardest test a floor takes. PEI 4 porcelain with a slight texture for grip, and a darker grout, is our default.

items.title: Covered porches
items.text: Only porcelain. Ceramic soaks up rain and a Puget Sound freeze pops the glaze off. Confirm the box says frost-resistant and pick a textured surface for wet-weather grip.

items.title: Radiant heat
items.text: Tile is the best floor over electric or hydronic radiant heat because it conducts and stores warmth. Porcelain is denser and moves less with temperature. Use an uncoupling membrane and a flexible thinset rated for heated floors.

blocks.html: Two specs on the box change the installation more than the material does.

items.html: Rectified edges. The tile is cut square after firing so every piece is exactly the same size. That allows grout joints of 1/16 to 1/8 in for a near-seamless look. Non-rectified tile varies slightly and needs 3/16 in joints or wider to hide it.

Large format means flatness. Any tile with a side over 15 in needs a subfloor flat to 1/8 in over 10 ft and 1/16 in over 2 ft. Otherwise you get lippage, one tile edge standing above its neighbor. Self-leveler or a mortar bed adds real cost on older Shoreline and Seattle floors.
Coverage and leveling. Large tile needs a large-format thinset, back-buttering and 95 percent mortar coverage in wet areas. Leveling clips are standard on 24 in and larger tile.
Plank tile has its own rule. Wood-look porcelain planks should be offset no more than one third, not a 50 percent brick pattern, or the slight crown in each plank creates lippage at every joint.

blocks.text: What drives the price of a tile floor

blocks.html: Wills Flooring quotes tile from a measured layout because these variables move the number more than the tile itself does.

items.html: Tile size and pattern. 12 by 24 straight-lay is the baseline. Herringbone, diagonal and small mosaics add cuts and time. Large format adds flatness prep.

Subfloor prep. Plywood needs a second layer or an uncoupling membrane; slabs need flatness checked and often leveled. This is the line that varies most between a 1970s Lynnwood split-level and a new build.
Demolition. Pulling old tile and thinset is slow and loud. Removing vinyl or carpet is quick.
Waterproofing and heat. Membranes in wet rooms and radiant mats under the tile each add material and a step.
Cuts and details. Toe kicks, curved walls, niches and floor drains all mean wet-saw time. Porcelain cuts slower than ceramic.

blocks.text: When ceramic is the smarter buy, and when neither is

a.title: Choose ceramic when
items: It is going on a wall or backsplash
A powder room or guest bath gets light, bare-foot traffic
Budget is tight and the room is dry
You want a hand-made or glazed look that only ceramic offers

b.title: Skip tile when
items: The subfloor bounces; tile and grout crack over deflection
You want warmth underfoot without radiant heat; vinyl plank or wood feel warmer
The floor must be redone quickly and cheaply in a rental
Plank flatness cannot be reached without major leveling

blocks.text: Mistakes we get called to fix

items.html: Ceramic on a porch or in a mudroom. It absorbs water, chips at the edges and shows the red body.
Large tile on an unflattened floor. Lippage you can catch a toe on, and no grout fixes it.
No membrane in a shower. Porcelain over bare drywall or plywood. The tile is fine; the wall behind it is rotting.
Wrong grout joint. Non-rectified tile forced into 1/16 in joints shows every size variation.

faq.q: Is porcelain tile better than ceramic for floors?
faq.a: For most floors, yes. Porcelain absorbs under 0.5 percent water, is denser and harder, and usually hides chips because the color runs through the body. Ceramic is fine for dry, light-traffic floors and walls, and it costs less and cuts more easily.

faq.q: What PEI rating do I need for a kitchen floor?
faq.a: PEI 3 for a normal kitchen, PEI 4 if you have dogs, kids or an entry door opening into the kitchen. PEI is a glaze wear test, so it applies to both ceramic and porcelain. Anything rated PEI 1 or 2 belongs on walls.

faq.q: Can ceramic tile be used in a shower?
faq.a: On the walls, yes. Ceramic wall tile is standard and comes in the widest range of colors. For the shower floor, use porcelain or a mosaic rated for wet floors with a slip-resistant surface. In both cases the waterproofing membrane behind the tile is what keeps the shower dry.

The edges are cut square after firing so every tile is exactly the same size. That allows tight grout joints of 1/16 to 1/8 in for a clean, modern look. Non-rectified tile varies slightly and needs wider joints to hide the difference.

faq.q: Why is large-format tile more expensive to install?
faq.a: Tiles over 15 in need a subfloor flat to 1/8 in over 10 ft, back-buttering, leveling clips and large-format mortar. The prep is the cost, especially on older Puget Sound homes with wavy plywood or uneven slabs.

faq.q: Does Wills Flooring publish a tile price per square foot?
faq.a: No. Tile pricing depends on size, pattern, subfloor prep, demolition and waterproofing more than on the tile itself, so we measure and quote each job in writing at a free in-home visit. You get one firm number before any work starts.
